purpose: Trace the general diet list cited by the Bauko pond-culture paper to its cited review, then assess directly observed diet evidence without presenting foreign invasive-population results as local Philippine diet.

taxon.nameScope: The sources use this species name. The Philippine rice-field and pond papers do not provide independently checkable vouchers or a species-identification procedure; this diet review does not resolve that separate identity question.

citationTrace.philippinePaperClaim: The 2019 introduction lists insect larvae, snails, worms, ostracods, cladocerans, fish eggs, algae and detritus, and cites Milton et al. (2018). The Bauko pond study did not examine stomach contents or measure diet.
citationTrace.secondarySourceAssessment: The 2018 article is a review, not a new local diet survey. It summarizes a broad omnivorous diet and mentions insect larvae, microcrustaceans, fish eggs, algae and detritus. Its own bibliography points to a mosquito-larvae feeding study and other sources; the listed items should not be described as observed in Bauko or throughout the Philippines.

primaryStudy.title: Diet of a cryptic but widespread invader, the oriental weatherfish (Misgurnus anguillicaudatus) in Idaho, USA
primaryStudy.citation: Urquhart, A. N., & Koetsier, P. (2014). Western North American Naturalist, 74(1), 92-98. https://doi.org/10.3398/064.074.0109.
primaryStudy.studyContext: An introduced/invasive population in water bodies connected to the Boise River, Idaho, USA; not a Philippine population or native-range study.
methodsAsReported: The authors caught 237 fish using baited minnow traps and examined stomach contents.
They report 158 empty stomachs, 42 containing only trap bait, and 37 with natural food items.
Diet summaries used gravimetric analysis, frequency of occurrence, mean percent by number, and graphical prey-specific abundance.
findingsAsReported: Macroinvertebrates were the primary diet component among the sampled population; chironomid larvae were the most numerous prey reported.
The authors describe the diet as generalized and suggest detritus is likely an important part. Treat the detritus statement as the authors' interpretation, not a measured Philippine diet result.

evidenceLimits: Only 37 of 237 sampled fish had natural food items in their stomachs; 42 stomachs contained only the bait used to catch them. The baited-trap method and high empty-stomach count limit generalization.
The results come from an introduced Idaho population and connected water bodies. They do not establish the diet of fish in Bauko, Mountain Province, or elsewhere in the Philippines.

The study supports a cautious species-level hypothesis of opportunistic feeding on small aquatic macroinvertebrates, especially chironomid larvae, with detritus possibly important in that population. It does not establish that all listed prey are eaten in every locality, season, life stage, or habitat.
No Philippine diet rows, bait recommendations, predator-prey interactions, fishing guidance, or public-app claims are supported by this review alone.

The broad food list in the Philippine paper is inherited from a secondary review; the cited list includes items not confirmed by the Idaho abstract as observed prey. Do not present the entire list as one directly measured result.

reuseReview.primaryStudyRepositoryStatement: Boise State University's ScholarWorks item page identifies the work as available under Creative Commons Attribution 3.0.
reuseReview.decision: Only an attributed concise summary of the repository metadata and abstract is recorded. No article PDF, tables, figures, or raw data are copied into the project.
reuseReview.secondaryReviewLicense: No item-specific reuse license was verified for the 2018 NIScPR-hosted review.

nextAction: A historical Japanese native-range gut-content study is now reviewed, but the evidence still does not establish Philippine local diet. Continue with recent native-range and Philippine stomach-content or field-feeding studies tied to identifiable specimens and a defined waterbody/season. Keep observed natural diet separate from bait suggestions; show geographic context, study method, and uncertainty.

sources.supports: The Philippine pond paper's general introductory food list and its citation of Milton et al. (2018); the paper itself did not measure diet.
The secondary-review context and its broad diet summary; not a local Philippine diet sample.

The peer-reviewed Idaho study context, baited-trap and stomach-content method, counts of empty/bait-only/natural-food stomachs, and abstract-level diet findings. The repository's linked PDF download was denied by the browser tool, so this review does not claim full-text or table-level extraction.
